one_liner: Hobby multithreaded AVX2 grep in Zig (zrep); self-reported 9.6x faster than GNU grep 3.12 on one log, near ripgrep.
what_it_does: A command-line grep replacement written in Zig (the search-result page lists the repository as 99.5% Zig) that searches files for a pattern and prints matching lines, with the usual -v, -c, -n and -o modes appearing in its benchmark table. The author calls it a hobby project to see 'how fast grep could really go if you stripped everything away and started from scratch'. It is a separate CLI, not a library, and its option coverage and regex dialect relative to GNU grep are not documented in anything reachable this session; a commit titled 'Add full regex engine with SIMD' shows a regex engine was added to an originally literal-focused tool.
how_it_is_fast: Per the README feature list (seen only through search-result summaries), it splits each file into line-aligned chunks and searches all chunks on every core at once with an AVX2-vectorised scanner. That is within-file parallelism, which GNU grep (single-threaded) and ripgrep (one thread per file, so one thread on a single large file) do not do. The source was not readable, so the exact substring algorithm (memchr-style first-byte filter, two-byte SIMD prefilter or other) and how output order is preserved across threads are unknown.
when_to_use: Experimenting with within-file parallel search of one very large, warm-cache log on a many-core x86-64 machine with AVX2, where the README's -v row (121 ms vs ripgrep 353 ms vs GNU grep 770 ms on a 205 MB log) shows the largest gap.
Reading as a compact Zig example of chunked, line-aligned multithreaded scanning with SIMD, if you can reach Codeberg or its zff.dev mirror.
Ad-hoc literal searches where only the standard -v, -c, -n, -o modes are needed and GNU grep compatibility does not matter.
when_not_to_use: As a GNU grep replacement in scripts: option coverage, regex syntax (BRE/ERE/PCRE), locale and binary-file handling, exit codes and context flags are not documented in anything reachable here.

When ripgrep is available: on the README's own 205 MB log ripgrep is faster with -n (33.6 ms vs 36.5 ms) and -o (33.4 ms vs 36.7 ms), ties with -c (38.1 ms vs 38.0 ms) and is only about 15% slower for plain output (38.4 ms vs 32.7 ms); ripgrep also has .gitignore handling, mature Unicode regex and a long track record.
Recursive searches over many small files (source trees): the single-file chunking is the advertised advantage, and no directory-walk numbers were readable this session.
Non-AVX2 CPUs or non-x86 platforms: the README advertises an AVX2 search and any fallback is not documented.
Production use generally: a hobby project with no visible release history, license contents not seen, and no independent measurement.

integration.dependencies: not documented (Zig toolchain only, as far as the search summaries show)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 advertised; other platforms not documented
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (CLI); runs multiple worker threads per file
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same basic grep usage and common flags (-v, -c, -n, -o) appear in its benchmark, but flag coverage and regex dialect versus GNU grep 3.12 are not documented

gotchas: Every figure here comes from search-engine summaries of the README: codeberg.org (proxy CONNECT 403 and DNS failure), its zff.dev mirror and the besthub.dev article were all unreachable this session, and there is no GitHub mirror, so the benchmark script, corpus, CPU model, zrep's Zig release mode and GNU grep's build and locale were never inspected.

The summaries attribute the 32.7 / 38.4 / 314 ms row to a 205 MB log with 706K matches of 'debug', while an earlier summary described a recursive /usr/include search, and a second table (271 MB, 2.5M-line log, output piped through cat to avoid GNU grep's /dev/null shortcut: zrep 76 ms vs ripgrep 198 ms vs GNU grep 248 ms) also exists; which methodology applies to which row is unverified.

In the 205 MB table zrep's count mode (-c, 38.0 ms) is slower than its full printing mode (32.7 ms), which is unusual since counting does strictly less work; it may mean the printing row's output sink differs (for example /dev/null or a pipe) from the count row, but the harness could not be read to check.

The headline gap over GNU grep compares a tool using all cores (the earlier summary says 28) within a single file against single-threaded GNU grep, so most of the 9.6x is parallelism rather than a better single-core matcher; against ripgrep, which is also effectively single-threaded on one file, the gap shrinks to 1.17x or reverses.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among catalogued grep-like tools, fastgrep (Rust, 3.7-9.9x over GNU grep 3.12 with a warm trigram index) and The Platinum Searcher are better documented, and xerg only beats BSD grep; pick zrep only to study or try within-file parallel scanning of a single huge log, and otherwise prefer ripgrep or fastgrep.
verified_claims_summary: Self-reported README numbers, read only through search summaries: on a 205 MB log with 706K matches of 'debug', warm cache, zrep 32.7 ms vs ripgrep 38.4 ms vs GNU grep 3.12 314 ms for normal output (about 9.6x over GNU grep, derived), -v 121 ms vs 353 ms vs 770 ms, -c 38.0 ms vs 38.1 ms vs 288 ms; CPU reported only as 28 cores, Zig build mode and GNU grep build and locale not stated.
status_note: Maintenance status unknown (last commit, release history and license text not reachable; a LICENSE file exists per search summaries); a hobby, reference-only project hosted on Codeberg with a zff.dev mirror, so treat its numbers as unverified until the README and benchmark script can be opened.
